strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: generative modeling of dynamic text-attributed graphs, as opposed to purely discriminative tasks. The construction of eight new datasets with genuinely rich node/edge text (compared to DTGB's identifier-like texts) is a valuable contribution to the community.

The introduction of two clearly delineated task formulations (TDGG and IDGG) captures a meaningful distinction between transductive and inductive dynamic graph generation, and mirrors realistic incremental growth patterns better than prior 'generate the final graph directly' approaches.

The proposed evaluation suite is genuinely multifaceted, combining structural (MMD, power-law), textual (LLM-as-judge across 5 criteria), and joint graph-embedding metrics, which is more holistic than prior BERTScore-only textual evaluation.

Extensive experiments across 4 LLM backbones, ablations (memory / reflection), comparisons to DGNN baselines on discriminative subtasks, and comparisons to existing generative baselines (VRDAG, DG-Gen) give a reasonably thorough empirical picture.
Scalability analysis and dataset statistics/documentation (licenses, degree/label distributions) are provided, aiding reproducibility and adoption.
The hub-node analysis and qualitative case studies provide some interesting, application-relevant insight into what the generative framework does and does not capture.
weaknesses: The core generative 'framework' (GAG-General) is largely an incremental extension of an existing method (GAG) to non-bipartite/general graphs; the technical novelty is limited to prompt engineering and pipeline generalization rather than a new model architecture, which somewhat undercuts the paper's claim of introducing a strong generative baseline.

The textual quality metric relies entirely on LLM-as-Evaluator (GPT) scoring the outputs of LLM-based generators, raising concerns about self-preference/circularity bias, especially since GPT-4o-mini is also one of the generation backbones being evaluated by presumably the same or a related model family.

Baselines for IDGG (VRDAG, DG-Gen) do not support textual generation at all, making the comparison between GAG-General and these baselines structurally lopsided (GAG-General is compared favorably on an axis - text - where competitors were never designed to compete); this weakens the claimed 'significant limitations of current approaches' conclusion.

No human evaluation is used to validate the LLM-as-Evaluator textual quality metric or the overall realism of generated graphs, despite text quality being a central claimed contribution of the benchmark.

The 'discriminative task' comparison for TDGG trains DGNNs on only 1,000 edges while comparing to GAG-General leveraging LLM world knowledge and much richer input context; this makes the comparison of 'generative vs. discriminative' somewhat apples-to-oranges and the claimed superiority of GAG-General may partly reflect unfair training-data starvation of baselines rather than genuine modeling superiority.

Some ablation/robustness details are unclear, e.g., how sensitive results are to hyperparameters like number of random walks, recall size, or temperature; no variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for any experiment, and given LLM stochasticity this is a notable gap for a benchmark paper.

Scalability results show significant time costs (tens of hours for even modest graph sizes) that raise questions about the practicality of GAG-General as an actual benchmarked baseline, though this is acknowledged as future work.

The graph embedding metric formulation (concatenating variable-length interaction histories, random projection) has questionable robustness/invariance properties (e.g., dependency on interaction ordering, degree-based dimensionality effects) which are not rigorously analyzed or validated against ground truth understanding of what 'good' scores should look like.

Presentation is dense with heavy reliance on appendix tables; some Table numbers in the main text appear potentially inconsistent given the volume of results, making thorough verification difficult for reviewers.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing DyTAG datasets (e.g., DTGB) have very sparse/low-quality node texts, and the paper curates eight new datasets with richer node and edge text across diverse domains (e-commerce, social, biography, citation, movie collaboration).

The TDGG/IDGG task formulations with an incremental, expansive generation protocol are a reasonable attempt to move beyond prior 'generate final graph directly' paradigms, and better reflect real-world graph growth.
Extensive appendix with implementation details, prompts, dataset documentation, and large tables of per-LLM-backbone results, which aids reproducibility in principle.
Multifaceted metric design (structural MMD/power-law, LLM-judged textual quality, embedding-based joint metric) attempts a holistic evaluation rather than relying on a single score.
weaknesses: Self-evaluation/circularity concern: GPT-4o-mini is used both as one of the four generator backbones and as the sole LLM-as-Evaluator for textual quality scoring, creating a plausible self-preference bias that is never discussed or controlled for (e.g., via multiple independent judges or human validation).

The comparisons against DGNN baselines (Tables 5-6, 30-32) and against VRDAG/DG-Gen (Table 10, 46) are not apples-to-apples: GAG-General leverages pretrained LLM world knowledge and rich text, while DGNNs/VRDAG/DG-Gen are trained from scratch on only 1,000 seed edges with no textual pretraining; using this to claim 'GAG-General outperforms SOTA discriminative/generative models' overstates the finding, since it mainly reflects LLM prior knowledge versus low-data training rather than a fair methodological advance.

VRDAG performs catastrophically poorly across every dataset (Degree MMD 0.7-0.9, near-zero graph embedding scores), which is suspicious and suggests possible under-tuned or mis-adapted baseline implementation rather than a genuine capability gap; no diagnostic analysis or sanity check is provided.

The proposed Graph Embedding Metric (extended JL-Metric) and the 5-criterion LLM-as-Evaluator textual metric are introduced without any validation that they correlate with actual generation quality or human judgment (e.g., no human study, no correlation analysis with ground truth deviations), undermining confidence that higher/lower scores reflect meaningful differences.

Results are reported as single runs throughout (no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds), despite LLM generation being stochastic (temperature 0.8), making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., ablation gains from memory/reflection) are statistically meaningful.

GAG-General's technical novelty is limited: it is explicitly described as an extension of the existing GAG framework with largely engineering-level generalizations (bipartite→non-bipartite, domain abstraction), and the paper never directly compares GAG-General against the original GAG baseline to substantiate the claimed improvements.

Practical utility of the framework is questionable given reported scalability: generating a 100k-edge graph takes ~16-18 hours and a 50k-edge IDGG graph takes ~28-36 hours, which is impractical for most benchmark or production use cases, yet this is understated in the main claims.

Dataset text quality itself is not independently validated (e.g., no human annotation study confirming semantic richness/correctness of crawled/augmented texts), so the 'high-quality textual features' claim rests mainly on text-length statistics rather than substantive quality assessment.

The 'Hub Node Analysis' in Section 5.3, used to argue practical value for e-commerce/marketing applications, is a single anecdotal example on one dataset without systematic evaluation, which is insufficient support for the broad claims made in the Future Work/Applications sections.

Selection of 'best of four LLM backbones' in several comparison tables (e.g., Tables 5, 6, 30) without clarifying the selection protocol raises concerns about cherry-picking when comparing against baselines.

strengths: Substantial and carefully curated dataset contribution: eight new DyTAG datasets spanning diverse domains (e-commerce, social media, biography, citation, movie collaboration) with genuinely rich node and edge text, addressing a real and well-documented gap in prior DyTAG benchmarks (e.g., DTGB's trivial username/email node texts).

Clear and well-motivated task formalization (TDGG and IDGG) that bridges discriminative and generative dynamic graph learning, with formal definitions, pseudocode, and a sensible transductive-to-inductive progression that mirrors real-world graph growth.

Multifaceted evaluation protocol combining structural (MMD, power-law), textual (LLM-as-judge across five criteria), and a joint graph-embedding metric (extended JL-metric) is a reasonable attempt at holistic assessment that goes beyond prior single-aspect metrics.

Extensive experimentation: four LLM backbones, ablations on memory/reflection mechanisms, comparisons against five DGNN baselines on discriminative subtasks and two dynamic graph generation baselines (VRDAG, DG-Gen), plus scalability analysis and dataset-quality validation experiments (Figure 2/6) demonstrating the practical benefit of better text quality.

The GAG-General framework generalizes the prior GAG system beyond bipartite social graphs, and the paper provides substantial reproducibility details (prompts, algorithms, hyperparameters, licenses) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Textual quality evaluation relies on an LLM-as-judge (GPT) that is also one of the four generators being evaluated, raising concerns about self-preference bias; no human evaluation or inter-rater reliability check is reported to validate the LLM-as-evaluator scores.

The discriminative-task comparisons (node retrieval, edge classification) train DGNN baselines on only 1,000 edges, which is an unusually small and likely unfair training budget for these methods; the resulting large gap in GAG-General's favor may primarily reflect this data-starved setup rather than genuine superiority of the generative paradigm, especially since GAG-General leverages LLM world knowledge and full node/edge texts not available to the DGNNs in this limited regime.

Scalability remains a serious practical limitation (e.g., 16–35 hours to generate 50k–100k edges), which is only lightly discussed; this restricts the benchmark's usability for the million-edge-scale datasets the paper itself highlights as a strength.

The IDGG 'hub node' analysis in Section 5.3 is largely anecdotal (three examples on one dataset) rather than a systematic quantitative validation of the claimed emergent/predictive capability, weakening the strength of the practical-application narrative.

No ablation isolating the specific architectural contributions of GAG-General relative to the original GAG (e.g., on a bipartite dataset where both are applicable) to substantiate the generalization/novelty claims beyond task formulation.

Reproducibility is partly dependent on proprietary APIs (GPT-4o-Mini) and large open LLMs (70B+), and result variance/costs of repeated LLM-based generation (e.g., due to sampling temperature 0.8) are not discussed, which may affect robustness of reported comparisons.
Some licensing terms (e.g., IMDB's restrictive commercial/redistribution terms) raise potential concerns about the benchmark's redistributability as claimed in the contribution statement.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: standardized benchmarks for generative (rather than merely discriminative) dynamic text-attributed graph learning.

Contributes eight new DyTAG datasets spanning diverse domains (bipartite and non-bipartite) with substantially richer node/edge text than prior datasets like DTGB, backed by quantitative comparisons (text length, perplexity, LLM-based ratings).

Clearly formalizes two new and meaningful tasks—TDGG (transductive) and IDGG (inductive)—that capture realistic incremental/expansive graph generation dynamics, rather than one-shot final-graph generation as in prior work.

Proposes a reasonably comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation protocol (structural MMD/power-law metrics, LLM-based textual quality scoring, and a graph-embedding similarity metric) tailored to the joint structural-temporal-textual nature of DyTAGs.

Extensive experimentation: multiple LLM backbones, ablations on memory/reflection mechanisms, comparisons against DGNNs and existing dynamic graph generation baselines (VRDAG, DG-Gen, TIGGER-I), scalability analysis, hub-node case studies, semantic-drift analysis, and a small human evaluation—demonstrating thorough empirical validation.
Strong reproducibility efforts: detailed dataset licensing, prompts, algorithm pseudocode, and stated intent to release code/data/leaderboard.
weaknesses: The core generative framework, GAG-General, is presented as a fairly incremental engineering extension of the prior GAG framework (removing the bipartite constraint, abstracting the pipeline) rather than a methodologically novel generative model; the paper's own framing acknowledges it is mainly a 'demonstration framework.'

Reliance on LLM-as-Evaluator for textual quality is potentially circular/self-reinforcing, since generation is also LLM-driven; possible biases of the evaluator LLM (even when backbone differs from generator) are not deeply analyzed or validated against human judgment beyond a small-scale check (50 samples, 5 annotators).

Discriminative-task comparisons against DGNNs use only a 1,000-edge training split, which may unfairly disadvantage DGNNs that are designed for larger-scale training, inflating the apparent advantage of the LLM-agent approach in low-data settings.

Scalability remains a significant practical limitation: generating even moderately sized graphs (e.g., 100K edges) takes 16+ hours, and IDGG scales worse (35+ hours for 50K edges), which curtails applicability to the large-scale million-edge datasets the benchmark itself provides.

The graph-embedding metric and memory/reflection mechanisms rely on several heuristic design choices (random walk-based memory, random projection for embedding alignment) without strong theoretical grounding or sensitivity analysis of these choices.
Some included datasets (e.g., IMDB) carry restrictive licensing terms that could complicate open benchmark distribution and reuse.

The generated graphs under IDGG show evidence of semantic drift (e.g., hub nodes diverging from platform-relevant categories) that is only partially mitigated via ad hoc prompt constraints, suggesting current framework robustness for open-ended generation is still limited.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-documented gap: existing DyTAG datasets (e.g., DTGB) have semantically poor node texts, and the paper provides reasonable quantitative evidence (PPL, LLM-rating) for this claim.
Introduces eight datasets spanning diverse domains (e-commerce, social, biography, citation, movie collaboration) with both bipartite and non-bipartite structures, which could be a useful resource.

Extremely thorough empirical exploration in the appendix: ablations across four LLM backbones, memory/reflection mechanisms, scalability tests, and comparisons to DGNN/dynamic graph generation baselines.
Attempts a holistic, multi-faceted evaluation protocol (structural, textual via LLM-judge, graph-embedding) for a task that genuinely lacks standardized evaluation.
weaknesses: GAG-General offers limited methodological novelty; it is an incremental, largely engineering-level extension of the prior GAG framework, which the authors themselves describe as merely a 'demonstration framework.'

The textual quality metric relies solely on LLM-as-judge scoring without robust validation against human judgment (only a small 50-sample, 5-annotator spot check with no inter-annotator agreement reported), raising concerns about reliability and potential bias.
The graph embedding metric (extended JL-Metric) lacks strong justification for why cosine similarity in a randomly projected space meaningfully captures generation quality.

Discriminative task comparisons in TDGG are unfair: GAG-General (leveraging a pretrained LLM's broad knowledge) is compared against DGNNs trained on only 1,000 edges, inflating apparent superiority rather than demonstrating genuine capability.

The GDGB vs. DTGB comparison (Section C.5) is circular, since it uses the authors' own GAG-General framework and self-designed metrics (co-developed with GDGB) to argue for GDGB's superiority, rather than independent validation.

Computational cost is very high (16+ hours for 100K edges) and most main experiments only generate 2K-10K edges from 1K seeds, far smaller than the million-edge scale of the proposed datasets, undermining claims of practical utility at scale.

IDGG-generated graphs frequently fail the power-law validity criterion and show substantially worse structural fidelity than TDGG, indicating the harder, more realistic task is not well solved by the proposed framework.

The paper's own semantic-drift analysis (Appendix F.14) shows topic drift after ~5K edges, and the proposed fix (manually injected domain constraints) is an ad hoc patch rather than a principled solution, raising robustness concerns.

Licensing of some source data (e.g., IMDB terms of use, Weibo-derived content) appears restrictive or ambiguous for redistribution of derived text-rich datasets, and the ethics statement is largely generic.
Core data-quality claims rely heavily on automated metrics (PPL, LLM rating) susceptible to length/fluency biases, without large-scale human evaluation to corroborate them.

strengths: Clear and important gap addressed: convincingly demonstrates that existing DyTAG datasets (e.g., DTGB) have textually impoverished nodes, backed by quantitative comparisons (PPL, LLM-based ratings, text length).

Substantial dataset contribution: eight diverse, carefully curated datasets spanning multiple domains (e-commerce, social, biography, citation, movie collaboration), covering bipartite and non-bipartite structures, with documented licensing and construction details.

Well-motivated task formulation: TDGG and IDGG sensibly bridge discriminative dynamic graph tasks with generative modeling, and IDGG's inductive node generation meaningfully models real-world graph growth.
Comprehensive, multi-faceted evaluation protocol combining structural MMD/power-law analysis, LLM-as-Evaluator textual quality metrics, and a graph-embedding-based joint fidelity metric.

Extensive experiments: multiple LLM backbones, ablations on memory/reflection mechanisms, comparisons against DGNN baselines and dedicated dynamic graph generation models, scalability analysis, downstream usability checks, data augmentation experiments, semantic drift analysis, and human evaluation.
Reproducibility effort: detailed prompts, algorithms/pseudocode, licenses, and stated intent to release code/data/leaderboard.

Fair comparison methodology: direct GDGB vs. DTGB comparison using the same GAG-General framework strengthens the claim that textual quality specifically benefits generative modeling rather than merely longer text.
weaknesses: GAG-General is somewhat incremental, mainly an engineering generalization of existing GAG (removing bipartite constraints, abstracting pipeline) rather than a methodologically novel generative model, as acknowledged by the authors themselves.

Metric validity concerns: the textual quality metric and part of the graph-embedding metric rely on LLM-as-Evaluator using GPT, which is also one of the generation backbones being evaluated, raising potential self-preference bias that is not discussed or controlled.
Limited new dynamic graph generation baselines for IDGG (VRDAG, DG-Gen, TIGGER-I), none of which handle text, making comparisons somewhat lopsided in favor of the text-aware GAG-General.

Scalability remains a real limitation: generating 100K edges takes 16+ hours and 50K edges in IDGG takes ~36 hours, questioning practical usability at the scale of the proposed million-edge datasets; this is left as future work.
IDGG structural fidelity is mixed, with several datasets failing power-law validity and showing notably worse MMD than TDGG, indicating non-trivial current framework limitations.
Small-scale human evaluation (50 samples, 5 annotators) with no inter-annotator agreement statistics limits validation of generative quality claims.
Asymmetric graph sizes used across TDGG (10K edges) and IDGG (2K edges) experiments make some structural comparisons less directly interpretable.

Dense presentation with most results deferred to a very long appendix, making it harder to assess core claims from the main text alone; some claims (e.g., 'groundbreaking performance') are stated more strongly than the mixed IDGG results fully support.
